# Offshore North
**Week ending:** August 10, 2026
> **Scott Shawyer has publicly stated his intention to compete in the 2028 Vendée Globe, the first Canadian to target a solo non-stop round-the-world race.**

## The Canadian Boat
Scott Shawyer, identified in recent coverage as the skipper of the Canada Ocean Racing Vendée Globe campaign, has stated his aim to enter the 2028 edition. No further details on boat acquisition, training schedule, or qualification plans were released by the campaign itself this week.

The public commitment keeps the Canadian entry visible on the 2028 entry list at a point when most IMOCA campaigns are already deep into qualification racing or boat programmes; any delay in securing a race-ready IMOCA now directly shortens the remaining two-year window to the 12 November 2028 start. With the start line fixed and the qualification period already open, the absence of a declared boat or entered races means the campaign must still convert the stated intention into measurable results in designated events before the points window closes. Every subsequent month without an IMOCA programme narrows the available calendar slots that award the required finishing points, and the class rules do not grant extensions for late entrants. Source: [The Globe and Mail](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMimwFBVV95cUxQeVJwV19wa1lZUTdkWElyT01EZ0RhVWVQTE1sS2VseHRrU2pzVEJncngwMFNibUlQMHlGN3c3ZnpDX3RIZXlGLWhiQ2Y3Zko0TXY0RG1zY2R6Ri0zaWpZakNvZ1UtOEtzbUxlTGh2emkzR2dHOWt6YkRUN1ltWFg3WGR2alZ6TWcxdWlGTEw2VWpjVllZamwxYUZpUQ?oc=5)

### The Fleet
Emirates Team New Zealand resumed AC75 sailing on 7 August after a two-month pause; the recon declaration sheet recorded no changes to component serial numbers. This keeps the current AC75 configuration as the baseline for the next design cycle and means any future modifications will be measured against an unchanged reference boat. The two-month lay-up had been expected to produce visible updates, yet the absence of new serial numbers indicates the team is still evaluating the existing platform before committing to hardware changes ahead of the next Cup cycle. Source: [sail-world.com](https://www.sail-world.com/news/298720/?source=rss)

Alicante has confirmed mobilisation of more than 40 boats for the start of The Ocean Race 2027. The larger entry list increases the number of crews that must be accommodated in the same port infrastructure and raises the operational complexity of the first leg compared with recent editions. Organisers must now coordinate berthing, safety checks and media access for a fleet size that exceeds the numbers seen in the immediately preceding editions of the event. Source: [Google News](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihAFBVV95cUxPME1SSTNoQk9SNFYzZVRxbmU2YjFHT2hEa1pkbEFlRkJmTkJ0Rk5QNEY3eVFCMUplaGFpb3VPYVAwZEFMb2puUUJOaXZKaTZOLUZhOWpuQjY2NTFHMjRvbW93VlpSVUMycEJBTGJKZWY2LThxUEdZUmtJdUtxbkVhcHJnc2s?oc=5)

Pierre Le Boucher has begun Route du Rhum preparation aboard Penfret. Early work on the IMOCA allows the team to test systems and crew routines well before the November start, shifting any major reliability issues from the race window into the current preparation period. The decision to begin fit-out and sea trials now spreads the workload across the remaining months rather than compressing it into the final weeks before the single-handed transatlantic departure. Source: [Google News](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiUEFVX3qxTE9OZFZIdU1ESXd1QU9zUklTUnl3ODJTN1d3dmtjbWM1blpINE1IbElLb3B3Ri1RVZpUQnNUZzg0SzQ2em9jMEpoc08zV3BDZVVm?oc=5)

World Sailing has placed four Olympic events under formal review for the 2032 Brisbane Games, including both kite and 470 classes. The review opens the possibility that current equipment or formats will be replaced, creating a multi-year uncertainty for sailors and builders who must decide whether to invest in the existing platforms. Recommendations will be considered at the 2026 Annual Conference, with options ranging from retention of the present gear to outright substitution by new formats. Source: [sailingscuttlebutt.com](https://www.sailingscuttlebutt.com/2026/08/06/going-on-the-offensive-to-avoid-removal/)

## Plain Sailing
Qualification for the Vendée Globe is a points-based system run by the IMOCA class. A skipper must accumulate a minimum number of points by finishing designated races in an IMOCA within a set period before the start; the exact points table and race list are published by the class and updated each cycle.

The system exists because the race is solo, non-stop and around the world. Organisers need evidence that every entrant has already managed an IMOCA alone for long distances and in varied conditions; a single training passage cannot supply that evidence, so results in named events are used instead. The chosen races typically include transatlantic and round-the-world courses that replicate the Southern Ocean demands the skipper will face, and only finishes within the qualification window count toward the total.

In practice this means a skipper without recent IMOCA miles must choose which qualifying races to enter and when, because the calendar is fixed and the points window closes months before the Vendée start. The choice directly determines whether a campaign can reach the start line at all. Missing a key points race because of a late boat delivery or an injury can leave a skipper short even if the boat itself is ready, forcing a last-minute scramble for an alternative event that may not award enough points to close the gap.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Most editions require at least two strong results in high-value races, and the points scale rewards both distance and difficulty. A podium in a shorter transatlantic event may deliver fewer points than a mid-fleet finish in a longer Southern Ocean leg, so skippers weigh the risk of damage against the reward of a higher-scoring result. Campaigns that already hold points from the previous cycle can sometimes coast; new entrants must build their entire tally inside the current window.

The rule also protects the race from untested boats and skippers. An IMOCA is a high-performance machine whose foils, rigs and electronics can fail dramatically when pushed for weeks on end. By requiring documented finishes, the class reduces the chance that an unprepared entry will need rescue in the Southern Ocean or create a hazard for the rest of the fleet. The same rule set that keeps the start list small also keeps the safety record strong.

For a new national campaign the practical effect is a compressed timeline. The skipper must locate a suitable IMOCA, complete any required refit, and then immediately begin accumulating results before the points deadline passes. Any gap between the public announcement and the first entered race shortens the available opportunities, because the class does not add extra events to accommodate late arrivals.

A listener could repeat this: qualification is not automatic once a boat exists; it is earned through specific race results inside a closing time window, and missing the points total keeps even a ready campaign off the Vendée start line.

## The Countdown
825 days remain until the Vendée Globe start on 12 November 2028. 
No sourced information yet establishes the Canadian campaign’s current qualification points or next scheduled race.

# Offshore North
**Week ending:** August 05, 2026
> **Six IMOCA teams will race The Ocean Race Atlantic 2026 with mandatory 50/50 gender parity crews, testing two new-generation boats ahead of the 2027 around-the-world edition.**

## What This Show Is
Offshore ocean racing ranks among the world's great endurance sports yet reaches English-speaking audiences mostly as late, partial results stripped of context. This show supplies the missing layer: it explains what each development actually changes for the boats, the sailors, and the campaigns that matter.

Every four years a handful of people attempt to sail alone, non-stop and unassisted around the world. No Canadian has ever finished that race. Scott Shawyer and Canada Ocean Racing are preparing to change that at the Vendée Globe that starts on 12 November 2028. The show follows their attempt week by week and uses it as the door into the wider sport.

Each episode keeps the same shape. The Canadian Boat section tracks only what the team itself has published and states the direct consequence for the 2028 qualification path. The Fleet section covers the rest of offshore racing with the same consequence test. Plain Sailing explains one concept so listeners can understand the week's news without prior expertise. The Countdown gives the exact number of days left and the current qualification status drawn only from sourced facts.

Sources are named and linked every week. No hype is added, no play-by-play is given that will be stale by Monday, and nothing is stated that the sources do not support. Uncertainty is flagged inline. The audience is assumed to be enthusiastic but not expert; every piece of jargon receives a single plain-language sentence on first use and is then left alone.

Offshore North is part of the Nerra Network, an independent, ad-free collection of daily shows produced by two friends and covering technology, science, markets, world news and language learning in several languages at nerranetwork.com.

## The Canadian Boat
Canada Ocean Racing issued no public updates this week.

**Standing item:** The next Vendée Globe starts on 12 November 2028; no Canadian skipper has yet completed the course.

Source: [no primary source this week]

### The Fleet
The Ocean Race Atlantic 2026 starts 1 September with six IMOCA entries sailing 3,600 nautical miles from New York to Lorient. Every crew must include two women, two men and one on-board reporter, creating the first 50/50 gender-parity offshore transatlantic race. The event serves as the main pre-event test before The Ocean Race round-the-world course begins in January 2027. Two new-generation IMOCAs already sailing will use the race as their first serious ocean test. Malizia 4 emerged from a three-team sistership collaboration between Team Malizia, TR Racing and Team Banque Populaire; it was designed by Antoine Koch with Finot-Conq and Gsea Design, is narrower and flatter than its predecessor, and carries more than 85,000 hours of build time. Skipper Boris Herrmann called the first week of sailing on the boat “love at first sail.” DMG MORI Global One follows a separate design route by Guillaume Verdier, built by Multiplast; its hull resembles the central hull of a trimaran and is intended to foil earlier while reducing slamming. Skipper Kojiro Shiraishi gave the designer the single brief “free mind, free ideas, no limits.” This race therefore supplies the first direct comparison between the two new boats under identical 50/50 crew rules and identical ocean conditions before the longer 2027 campaign. Source: [sailingscuttlebutt.com](https://www.sailingscuttlebutt.com/2026/08/03/imocas-prepare-for-transatlantic-sprint/)

British America's Cup team GB1 has added kitefoiler Jemima Lines (née Crathorne) to its sailing squad. The announcement brings recent high-speed foiling experience directly into a campaign that will require precise handling of its eventual Cup boat. Lines joins an existing squad that must integrate new talent across multiple disciplines before the next Cup cycle. The move is a concrete personnel step rather than a results announcement, reflecting the multi-year timeline on which Cup teams assemble and train crews. No further details on her specific role or schedule were released with the announcement. Source: [sail-world.com](https://www.sail-world.com/news/298590/?source=rss)

## Plain Sailing
Gender parity rules require mixed crews on offshore boats. In The Ocean Race Atlantic 2026 the rule is explicit: two women, two men and one on-board reporter on every entry. The requirement is not a suggestion; it is written into the notice of race and applies to every team that wants to start.

The rule changes how campaigns select sailors and how they train. A skipper can no longer fill a five-person watch system with the four most experienced offshore sailors available; at least two of those sailors must be women who meet the same physical and skill thresholds as their male teammates. That constraint affects hiring timelines, training blocks and even boat layout, because watch systems and berthing must now accommodate the mandated balance rather than the fastest available combination.

The practical effect is that teams must develop a wider bench of qualified offshore sailors earlier in the campaign cycle. For the two new IMOCAs already launched, the rule also means their first serious ocean miles will be sailed by crews that were assembled under the parity constraint rather than under an open selection process. The single sentence a listener could repeat is: the rule forces every team to solve the same talent-pool problem at the same time.

An IMOCA is a 60-foot monohull built to a strict class rule that permits foils, water ballast and other performance features while capping overall length, beam and other dimensions. The class rule itself does not dictate crew composition; that decision belongs to each race organiser. When an organiser adds a gender-parity clause, the constraint travels with the entry list rather than with the boat design. Teams therefore face two parallel problems: they must still optimise the boat for solo or short-handed sailing in later events, yet they must also prove the same boat works with a five-person mixed crew on the Atlantic course. The on-board reporter counts toward the total but does not sail the boat, so the four sailing positions must still satisfy the two-plus-two split. This creates a narrow window in which teams can test new equipment and new crew combinations simultaneously. Because the race starts on 1 September, any shortfall in qualified female offshore sailors must be solved before that date; there is no later qualifying event that can substitute for the experience these crews will gain. The same calendar pressure applies to every entry, which is why the rule is described as the first 50/50 gender-parity crewed transatlantic race in offshore sailing.

## The Countdown
830 days remain until the Vendée Globe start on 12 November 2028. 
The Canadian campaign's qualification status is not established in this week's sources; the next scheduled milestone is the start itself.
